replies.content: Our performance reviews are built around five key pillars, each designed to foster growth, accountability, and excellence within our team: 1. Work Quality We evaluate the accuracy, consistency, and efficiency of your work. This includes attention to detail, meeting or exceeding standards, and overall contributions to the team's success. Metrics such as legitimate callbacks, customer reviews, and completed tasks are key indicators of quality. 2. Communication and Listening Skills Effective communication is vital in every role. We assess your ability to clearly and professionally convey information, actively listen, and respond constructively to feedback. Specific focus areas include: Being a team player versus confrontational behavior. Interaction with customers and troubleshooting issues independently before escalating to management. 3. Attendance and Punctuality Reliability is crucial for operational efficiency. We measure your ability to: Clock in and out accurately. Arrive on time for shifts and appointments. Complete jobs within the scheduled timeframe in Jobber to maintain workflow efficiency. 4. Initiative Proactive contributions drive the company forward. We look for team members who take ownership of their work and actively seek opportunities to add value. Specific examples include: Capturing before-and-after photos of completed jobs. Setting up lawn signs and distributing 5-arounds (brochures/door hangers) to nearby homes to increase visibility. 5. Dependability Dependable employees inspire confidence and trust. This includes consistency in meeting commitments, maintaining a positive attitude under pressure, and adhering to company standards. Key factors include: Keeping your vehicle clean and organized. Demonstrating driver accountability. Maintaining proper uniform and appearance. Ensuring no tools or equipment are left behind at the shop or job site. By focusing on these core criteria, we ensure a fair, detailed review process that highlights individual strengths, identifies areas for improvement, and supports ongoing professional development. This structured approach helps us maintain a high-performing team dedicated to delivering exceptional results.

As we hit certain break points we know that to take on more crew staff will require additional office staff to help manage. We then look at the profit of each crew minus the increase in office staff to manage them. We have found over the years that expansion is not always the best if you end up having more staff but no more profit.

replies.author: julie
replies.content: JOBBER COMMUNITY TEAM to Coppo Thanks for sharing your experience—it’s impressive to hear from a business that’s been around since 1971! Your approach to balancing crew and office staff is a great reminder that growth doesn’t always mean adding more people if it’s not driving profit.

replies.author: GBPlumbing
replies.content: to Coppo Thank you for this, we definitely agree to always looking at your numbers first. And you said there has to be a balance of work crews to then office staff. You don't want to over run your administration staff.

replies.author: MrShortbuster
replies.content: to Coppo Let me just jump in to add that I've found "Markup and profit a contractors guide" by Mike stone to be an incredible resource for this. He walks through all the basic contractor math and shows exactly how to calculate the effect on markup of hiring additional staff (or any other overhead expense). He does a really good job showing you how to work the math backwards and forwards to figure out either A. what your markup needs to be to sustain certain expenses (such as additional office staff) or B. what additional sales volume is required to make the new expense work at the same company markups. There are lots of resources out there that cover this type of material but I can say hands down that Mike Stone's books are the best. I also recommend profitable sales, he's got a book on estimating as well but I don't find that one to be as valuable as "Profitable Sales" and "Markup and Profit". Those two books are always close at hand for keeping the knowledge fresh.

replies.author: AdamSylvester
replies.content: It sounds it's time to hire for a 4th truck. What's the hesitation?

replies.author: ShlomoS
replies.content: Don't always assume that just because you're running around a chicken without a head, that you need to hire more employees. Try determining what every employee should bring in monthly. make sure you hit that goal consistently before hiring more. for example, if all of your employees do the same services and hold the same position, and you expect each one to produce, lets say $30k per month, then you would not outfit a fourth truck until you were consistently reaching or exceeding $90k a month. you may find that you are super busy, but it may be due to inefficiency, routing issues, new guy mistakes, and follow-ups. the way to confirm you are on track is by ensuring each truck is making what it should make before growing.

replies.author: julie
replies.content: JOBBER COMMUNITY TEAM to ShlomoS Great insights! I love the idea of making sure your team is producing a consistent revenue before adding more staff. Focusing on efficiency and profitability can really help avoid the common pitfalls of growing too quickly.

replies.author: GBPlumbing
replies.content: to ShlomoS Thank you for your insight. We definitely agree to always look at your numbers first, and make sure everything and everyone is running efficiently before hiring.

replies.author: BobScotland
replies.content: There are 3 main things you need to balance: 1) Your production vs non-production staff ratio (talked about earlier in the thread, for us its 5:1) - 2) Add up the hours your production teams are working per week and divide it by your base hours per worker (in our case its 35 hours per week but for many its 40 hours); this simple sum will give you how many workers you might need to cover the work available - 3) Finally, look at your production pipeline; are you going to sustain the level of business you currently have (in our case we are seasonal) - Hope this helps

replies.author: Conrad

title: Hiring early? Benefit or hinderance?
author: peterz3g
content: Is it more effective to hire during the slow season, allowing ample time for thorough training while accepting the risk of reduced working hours for new team members, or is it better to focus on hiring quickly during the busy season to meet immediate demand but potentially sacrifice the depth of training? What factors, such as employee retention, operational efficiency, and service quality, should be prioritized in making this decision? CLEANING FINDING EMPLOYEES GENERAL HIRING TIPS TRAINING

replies.author: DTDL-Admin
replies.content: Hey Peterz3g, We’ve found it works best in our case to hire during the slow season whenever possible. (Small landscaping business.) It gives us time to properly train new team members without the pressure of that peak demand. And while hours might be lighter at times, it pays off with stronger retention, bonding our team, better service quality, and a smoother workflow when things get busier for us. Hiring mid-season can fill immediate gaps we have pop-up, but it often comes at the cost of rushed training and long-term consistency. For us, it’s about building a solid team who can put out consistent, quality work. Great question.

replies.author: LukeSalmonArm
replies.content: to DTDL-Admin I totally agree with hiring in the slow season. Depending on your industry, having enough time to properly train new hires is critical. I always underestimate both how long on-boarding takes and how little time I'll have during busy season, so hiring in slow season really helps. You just have to make sure that you have the cash-flow to cover the added wages!

replies.author: kimberlyg2g
replies.content: Thats the million dollar questions. I try to hire before I need an employee but am getting close. From interview to orientation to finishing training for us it is 3-4 weeks. Having to hire in a rush means you often skip over some yellow flags because your schedule is full. We are primarily a cleaning business. I am always very honest about what their schedule cold be and never over promise hours.

replies.author: Jennifer
replies.content: I find that I approach hiring with an all the time mentality now. I am always on the look for the next employee when Im out and around. We have successfully head hunted a few amazing people who were not being treated well where they were employed. Wherever possible I am hoping to hire and train these people in the off season but if I find someone amazing I will usually try to bring them in asap. I also live by the hire fast fire fast motto now and it has helped a lot
